title: Fiona the hippo’s death was tragic. But blaming a ‘bad mom’ is absurd | Arwa Mahdawi
text:
“Do they know the identity of the mother of the boy with the hat Fiona swallowed??” asks one Facebook post with thousands of likes. “She should be charged!!”
Spend a few minutes scrolling social media, and you will find endless variations of this statement. On Thursday, Fiona, a beloved hippo, died after eating a hat that had fallen into her enclosure at the Cincinnati zoo. Now a lot of angry people are out for blood.
By all accounts, Fiona’s death was a freak accident. A visitor, thought to be a small child, tossed a hat into the air. It was caught by a ceiling fan which launched it in just the right direction through a 1ft opening in the hippo’s viewing windows. Fiona ingested the hat, causing fatal medical complications that won’t be entirely clear until a post-mortem.
“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” a zoo spokesperson, Michelle Curley, said in a statement to Axios about this unfortunate sequence of events.
But while Fiona’s death may have been a tragic accident, social media mobs are desperate to find someone to blame. And the obvious scapegoat is the mother. She should have disciplined her bratty child! She should have taken the hat away from the kid! She should have been a better parent!
We’ve seen almost this exact story play out before.
Ten years ago, authorities killed a 17-year-old gorilla called Harambe after a three-year-old boy crawled into the enclosure at Cincinnati Zoo. The child’s mother, who had her hands full with three other kids when the incident occurred, was identified by name and immediately became the target of an online witch-hunt. More than 500,000 people signed a petition asking for her to be held accountable, and she was mercilessly harassed. Nobody seemed to ask where the father was.
Harambe’s death was a slightly different set of circumstances from Fiona’s. Nevertheless, the reaction demonstrates a social impulse to blame mothers for anything and everything involving their children.
“Blaming mothers is automatic, almost instinctive,” the legal scholar Linda Fentiman wrote of the Harambe case at the time. “The tendency to blame mothers for all potential and actual harm to their children is deeply imbedded in our psyche, our culture, and our legal system.”
Mothers are held to impossibly high standards and: “When any mortal mom is compared to the perfect mother, she is likely to be found wanting, and thus, potentially negligent.”
Fentiman added that there is a “growing trend in American society to seek a legal remedy for many accidents or unfortunate incidents which previously would have been viewed simply as bad luck”. It’s more comforting, after all, to have someone to blame than to face the fact that life can be random and cruel.
And mother-blaming goes well beyond fatal zoo incidents. From the 1950s to the 1970s, autism was blamed on “refrigerator mothers” who were emotionally cold and distant from their child. Now that’s been discredited, but there’s plenty more junk science out there. Last year, the Trump administration distorted scientific studies to claim that there was a link between women using Tylenol while pregnant and autism in children.
Mother-blaming is also deeply embedded in legal systems around the world. A report published this year analyzed 91 published family law judgments in England and Wales and found “mothers’ behaviour [was] scrutinised intensely while the fathers’ conduct was contextualised or minimised”.
None of this, to be clear, is to say that mothers, and parents more generally, shouldn’t ever be held accountable for their offspring’s actions.
As anyone who has set foot in a public space recently can confirm, there are a lot of parents out there who seem unwilling to set any boundaries for their children. I, for one, will never forget being trapped on a transatlantic flight with a child who would not stop playing their screechy recorder.
Forget everything I’ve said about institutionalized misogyny in the legal system: straight to jail for that mother.
Elon Musk says he’s not Maga and feels foolish about midterm spending
Regrets: Elon Musk has a few. The world’s richest person denied being Maga this week, adding: “I’m not sure what Maga means.” I’m pretty sure it means wearing a custom Maga hat, aligning yourself with Donald Trump’s Maga policies, accompanying the president on state trips, and spending obscene amounts of money propping up Maga candidates.
Why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
“We’re living through a global crisis of loneliness, with the World Health Organization declaring it a priority for public health, but it’s hard to miss that the coverage and conversation has been overwhelmingly focused on men,” writes Elle Hunt.
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority
The international court of justice (ICJ) found that the 2016-2017 military campaign by Myanmar targeting its Rohingya minority amounted to genocide in a landmark ruling. “Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to ‘prevent births’,” the Guardian reports. “Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.”
Seventy–two-year-old Palestinian woman killed by Israeli militants
Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in the occupied West Bank when she shot in the head after Israeli settler militants fired towards Palestinian houses.
One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage
Forty-five percent of women in west and Central Africa have no power of consent, according to a new report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). In east and southern Africa and in Arab states, 33% of women are also unable to say no to their partner.
Nearly one in four children now live in conflict zones
A new report by Save the Children found the highest number of children living in conflict zones since records began in 1990. Africa is home to 44% of the global total, a nearly 20% increase from 2024. The report found the fastest-growing grave violation against children is the denial of humanitarian aid. More than 70% of all verified aid denial last year took place against Palestinian children.
Melania Trump has a new docuseries out
“Calling Melania thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry,” writes Stuart Heritage who bravely endured the entire documentary. “There are times when even the interviewer palpably gives up.”
Joe Biden told Netanyahu he loved and admired him in final call from White House
The Jerusalem Post reported that it obtained a transcript of Biden’s last conversation with accused war criminal Benhamin Netanyahu. “I can’t tell you how much I appreciate you and what you’ve been through,” Biden said. “I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.” Want to spell out exactly what Netanyahu did, Joe? He has the blood of tens of thousands of dead Palestinian kids on his hands. Dropping 2,000lb bombs on tent camps full of starving people isn’t exactly how I’d define “courage”.
‘Parents are up in arms over school photos that look like mug shots’
So says the Wall Street Journal, which reports: “We’re in the midst of a no-smile epidemic” amongst school-age children. While I’d take all this with a pinch of imported German rock salt, there are some fun nuggets here about how social media trends are impacting school photos. “[M]ale students are tilting their head backwards,” one staff photographer told the WSJ. “They tell me they are ‘aura farming.’ I had to look it up.” I had to look it up too.
- Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist
